topic: Day 2 · Systems, Transitions & Prevention — Closing the Loop
speakerTitle: Consultant in Diabetes & Endocrinology and Inpatient Diabetes Lead
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Diabetes & Endocrine Unit
speakerBio: Diabetes lead for the inpatient service and JBDS-guideline evangelist who is convinced that most preventable DKA readmissions are engineered at the discharge desk on a Friday afternoon.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted in DKA, treated beautifully by the book, and discharged 36 hours later at 5 p.m. on a Friday. Nobody restarted her long-acting insulin before the IV insulin came down; her follow-up letter went to the wrong GP; and no one asked why she had run out of insulin in the first place (she couldn't afford the prescription and had been rationing). Nine days later she was back in DKA. The clinical care in the middle was excellent. The system around it — the transition off IV insulin, the discharge, the education, the follow-up — failed at every seam. This closing session is about the seams, because that is where diabetes patients fall through, and it is where a whole conference of good medicine is either delivered or wasted.

1 · 📦 DKA/HHS care bundles and the specialist team

The great advance of the last decade in inpatient diabetes was not a new drug — it was standardised care bundles. The JBDS-IP (Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care) guidelines turned DKA and HHS management into checklists that any team can follow safely:

  • Fixed-rate weight-based IV insulin (~0.1 units/kg/hr), continue the long-acting basal insulin throughout, monitor ketones/bicarbonate/glucose hourly, and add glucose substrate (10% dextrose) once glucose falls below ~14 mmol/L — resolving the ketoacidosis, not just the glucose.
  • HHS is a different beast: slower, fluid-led correction, cautious insulin (often only after fluids), vigilance for osmotic shifts, and a high VTE risk warranting thromboprophylaxis.
  • Refer every DKA/HHS admission to the specialist diabetes inpatient team — specialist review reduces length of stay, errors and readmission. The bundle gets them out of the crisis; the specialist team stops them coming back.
💡 The bundle mindset

Care bundles work because they remove reliance on any one clinician remembering everything at 3 a.m. Treat DKA/HHS, insulin prescribing, and the sick-day pathway as protocolised systems — and audit whether the protocol was actually followed, because 'we have a guideline' and 'we followed the guideline' are different statements.

2 · 🔌 Safe transition off IV insulin — the classic disaster point

The single most dangerous moment in inpatient diabetes is stopping the IV insulin infusion. IV insulin has a half-life of minutes; the moment it stops, the patient has no insulin on board unless a subcutaneous depot is already established. Get this wrong and a resolved DKA relapses on the ward.

⚠️ The overlap rule

Give the first dose of subcutaneous long-acting (basal) insulin 30–60 minutes BEFORE the IV infusion is switched off, so a depot is absorbing before the drip stops. Convert only when the patient is eating and drinking, ketones cleared and acidosis resolved. Ideally transition alongside a meal and its prandial bolus. If the patient never stopped their usual basal (as the bundle advises), the bridge is already partly built — but you still confirm the basal is running before the IV comes down. Stopping IV insulin with no overlap is a re-DKA generator.

3 · 🚪 Safe discharge — restart, overlap, follow-up

A safe diabetes discharge is a checklist, not a signature:

  1. Restart the patient's usual medications deliberately — reconcile everything held during the admission (metformin, SGLT2 inhibitor, etc.) and document what to restart and when, so nothing is silently omitted or dangerously resumed.
  2. Confirm the insulin regimen is the right one and the patient can deliver it — correct product, device, and enough supply to get home and through the weekend.
  3. Ensure basal cover is established before discharge if they were on IV insulin.
  4. Arrange follow-up — diabetes specialist nurse contact, GP letter to the right GP, and structured education referral.
  5. Address the precipitant — why did they present? Missed insulin, infection, new diagnosis, psychosocial crisis, cost? An unaddressed precipitant is a booked readmission.

4 · 📚 Structured education and SICK-DAY RULES — the biggest readmission preventer

If you teach a diabetic patient one thing before discharge, teach the sick-day rules. Nothing else prevents more DKA readmissions. The core rules:

Sick-day ruleWhy it matters
NEVER stop your insulin, even if you are not eatingIllness raises insulin requirements; stopping basal precipitates DKA — the commonest avoidable cause
Check blood glucose more often (every 2–4 hours)Requirements swing during illness; catch the rise early
Check blood/urine KETONES when unwell or hyperglycaemicKetones are the early warning of impending DKA — before you feel terrible
Keep hydrated — sip fluids regularlyIllness + osmotic diuresis dehydrates fast; prevents the pre-renal spiral
Take extra correction insulin per an agreed plan if glucose/ketones riseExtra rapid-acting insulin heads off ketosis
Know WHEN to seek help — persistent vomiting, rising ketones, can't keep fluids downThe threshold that turns a manageable illness into a hospital admission
Sick-day rules in one line: when you are ill, never stop insulin, check ketones, keep drinking, and know when to call for help. That sentence prevents more DKA than any drug on the ward.
💡 Structured education works

Structured self-management education (type 1 programmes such as DAFNE, and type 2 equivalents such as DESMOND) improves outcomes and reduces crises. Education is not a leaflet handed over at discharge — it is a referred, structured intervention. Every DKA admission is a signal that the patient's self-management support needs strengthening.

5 · 📡 Technology — CGM, flash and closed-loop

Diabetes technology is now a frontline tool for preventing the crises the rest of this conference has been treating:

TechnologyWhat it doesRole in preventing crises
Flash glucose monitoring (e.g. Libre)Scan/continuous interstitial glucose, trend arrows, no routine fingersticksCatches rising or falling trends early; improves engagement and time-in-range
Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)Real-time interstitial glucose with alarms for high/lowAlarms rescue hypoglycaemia unawareness — a warning the neuropathic patient has lost; reduces severe hypos
Hybrid closed-loop ("artificial pancreas")CGM + pump + algorithm auto-adjusting basal insulinIncreases time-in-range, reduces hypos and glycaemic variability; a major advance for brittle/hypo-prone patients
🎯 Technology and hypo unawareness

For the patient who has lost their adrenergic warning symptoms (session 15), a CGM with low-glucose alarms is a genuine safety net — the technology supplies the warning the autonomic nervous system no longer can. This is one of the highest-value uses of CGM and a strong indication in guidelines.

6 · 🔁 Recurrent admissions and the psychosocial drivers

A small number of patients account for a large share of DKA admissions, and the driver is usually not a knowledge gap you can fix with a leaflet. Look for:

  • Insulin omission — deliberate or from cost, access, needle phobia, eating disorders ("diabulimia"), or mental illness.
  • Socioeconomic barriers — cannot afford prescriptions/supplies, housing instability, no fridge, chaotic circumstances.
  • Psychological burden — depression, diabetes distress, disordered eating — all strongly linked to recurrent DKA.
💡 Ask "why", not just "what"

The recurrent-DKA patient does not need to be told again how to manage diabetes — they usually know. They need someone to ask why it keeps failing, and to bring in the diabetes specialist nurse, psychology, social support and safeguarding as needed. Treating the ketoacidosis without addressing the driver guarantees the next admission.

7 · 📊 Quality metrics — reducing hypoglycaemia and DKA readmission

What gets measured gets improved. The inpatient diabetes quality metrics worth tracking:

  • Inpatient hypoglycaemia rate (especially severe/nocturnal, and insulin-related medication errors).
  • DKA/HHS readmission rate — a direct measure of discharge and education quality.
  • Insulin prescribing error rate and adherence to the "units-in-full" standard (session 13).
  • Proportion of DKA/HHS reviewed by the specialist team.
  • Length of stay and time to specialist referral.
  • Bundle compliance — was the JBDS pathway actually followed?

8 · 🧵 Synthesis — closing the loop on the whole conference

Across sixteen sessions the thread has been the same: diabetes emergencies are systems problems as much as biochemical ones. Pull the loop closed:

  • Diagnose and treat the crisis by the bundle — DKA, HHS, hypoglycaemia — resolving acidosis and ketones, not just glucose (early sessions).
  • Prescribe insulin safely — 'units' in full, right product/route, mind the pump's missing basal depot (s13).
  • Curate the drug chart in acute illness — hold metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, sulfonylureas appropriately; protect the type 1 basal (s14).
  • Hunt the emergencies diabetes hides — silent MI, the red hot foot, fulminant infection, autonomic ambushes (s15).
  • Then close the loop — safe transition off IV insulin, deliberate restart of held drugs, sick-day education, technology for the hypo-unaware, address the psychosocial driver, and measure your readmissions (this session).
Great inpatient diabetes care is not one heroic decision — it is a chain of reliable systems, and the patient is only as safe as the weakest seam. Close every seam.
☠️ M&M — the perfect admission, the failed discharge

A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes was admitted in DKA and managed flawlessly by the JBDS bundle: fixed-rate insulin, basal continued, ketones cleared, out in 36 hours. But the discharge fell apart at every seam. The IV insulin was stopped at 4 p.m. and her subcutaneous basal was written up but not given before the drip came down, leaving an insulin gap. She left at 5 p.m. on a Friday with three days of insulin and a follow-up letter addressed to a GP she'd left two years earlier. Nobody explored why she had presented — she had been rationing insulin because she could not afford the prescription charges and had told no one. No sick-day education, no DSN contact, no social referral. Nine days later she was readmitted in DKA. Root causes: unsafe transition off IV insulin (no overlap); a rushed Friday-afternoon discharge with inadequate supply and wrong follow-up; no structured sick-day education; and — the real one — a failure to ask why, missing a modifiable psychosocial and financial driver. The medicine in the middle was textbook. The system around it readmitted her. Closing the loop is the treatment.

9 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Use the JBDS DKA/HHS bundles and refer every case to the specialist diabetes team — protocols, not memory, and specialist review cuts readmission.
  2. Transition off IV insulin is the danger point — give SC basal 30–60 min BEFORE stopping the infusion, only once eating and non-ketotic.
  3. A safe discharge is a checklist — restart held meds deliberately, confirm insulin supply and device, right follow-up, and address the precipitant.
  4. Sick-day rules are the single biggest readmission preventer — never stop insulin, check ketones, hydrate, know when to seek help.
  5. Technology prevents crises — CGM alarms are a safety net for hypoglycaemia unawareness; closed-loop improves time-in-range.
  6. Recurrent admissions are usually psychosocial — ask 'why', not 'what', and bring in DSN, psychology and social support.
  7. Measure hypoglycaemia and DKA readmission — close the loop from the crisis all the way back to prevention.

moderatorQs.q: Talk us through exactly how you convert a patient from an IV insulin infusion to subcutaneous insulin without precipitating a relapse.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The core danger is that IV insulin has a half-life of minutes, so the instant the infusion stops the patient has no insulin on board unless a subcutaneous depot is already absorbing. The rule is overlap: give the first dose of subcutaneous long-acting basal insulin 30–60 minutes before you switch off the drip, so the depot is established when the IV stops — and ideally time the changeover with a meal and its prandial rapid-acting bolus. Only convert when the patient is eating and drinking, ketones have cleared and the acidosis has resolved. If, as the JBDS bundle advises, the usual basal was never stopped, the bridge is already partly built — but you still confirm the basal is running before the IV comes down. Stopping the infusion with no overlap is a classic way to send a resolved DKA straight back into relapse on the ward.

moderatorQs.q: You have one shot at educating a patient before a DKA discharge. What do you prioritise, and why that?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The sick-day rules, because nothing else prevents more DKA readmissions. The essentials: never stop your insulin even when you are not eating (illness raises requirements, and stopping basal is the commonest avoidable DKA trigger); check glucose more frequently and check ketones when unwell or hyperglycaemic (ketones warn you before you feel terrible); keep hydrated; take extra correction insulin per an agreed plan; and know the threshold to seek help — persistent vomiting, rising ketones, inability to keep fluids down. I would also make sure they leave with adequate insulin supply, the right device, correct follow-up, and a referral to structured education (DAFNE/DESMOND), because a leaflet is not education. That one conversation prevents more DKA than any drug on the ward.

moderatorQs.q: A patient is on their fourth DKA admission this year. Everyone rolls their eyes and re-teaches carb counting. What are they missing?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: They are missing that recurrent DKA is almost always a psychosocial problem, not a knowledge gap — the patient usually already knows how to manage their diabetes. The real driver is typically insulin omission from cost or access barriers, needle phobia, disordered eating ('diabulimia'), depression or diabetes distress, or chaotic social circumstances (no fridge, housing instability, unaffordable prescriptions). Re-teaching carb counting for the fourth time changes nothing. The task is to ask 'why does it keep failing?' and mobilise the right team — the diabetes specialist nurse, clinical psychology, social work and safeguarding — and address the modifiable driver. Treating the ketoacidosis without addressing the reason just books the next admission.

audienceQs.q: It's Friday afternoon and my DKA patient is medically ready. What do I actually check before I let them go?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Run a discharge checklist, not a signature. Confirm: (1) they are eating, drinking, non-ketotic and off IV insulin with an established subcutaneous basal (basal given before the drip stopped); (2) their usual medications held during admission are deliberately restarted or a clear plan documented; (3) they have the correct insulin product, device and enough supply to cover the weekend; (4) follow-up is arranged — DSN contact and a GP letter to the correct GP, plus a structured-education referral; and (5) you have addressed why they presented and delivered sick-day rules. A Friday-afternoon discharge with three days of insulin, no education and the wrong follow-up is how patients bounce back within days.

audienceQs.q: Which patients should I be pushing hardest to get onto CGM, from a crisis-prevention angle?
audienceQs.answerHTML: From a pure safety angle, prioritise those where the technology supplies a warning the patient has lost or can't get: above all patients with hypoglycaemia unawareness — often from autonomic neuropathy — for whom a CGM with low-glucose alarms is a genuine safety net that catches falls the adrenergic system no longer signals. Also high-value: recurrent severe hypoglycaemia, brittle/highly-variable type 1, recurrent DKA, and pregnancy. Real-time CGM (with alarms) is preferable to intermittently-scanned flash for the hypo-unaware, and for the most unstable, escalation to a hybrid closed-loop system meaningfully improves time-in-range and cuts hypos. These are exactly the patients who otherwise generate the crisis admissions.

audienceQs.q: If I want to improve inpatient diabetes safety, which metrics are worth putting on the dashboard?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Track the ones that map onto real harm and onto the failure points this conference covered: inpatient hypoglycaemia rate (especially severe and nocturnal episodes and insulin-related medication errors), the DKA/HHS readmission rate (a direct read-out of discharge and education quality), insulin prescribing error rate including adherence to writing 'units' in full, the proportion of DKA/HHS cases reviewed by the specialist diabetes team, JBDS bundle compliance (was the pathway actually followed, not just available), and length of stay / time to specialist referral. Pairing a process measure (bundle compliance, specialist review) with an outcome measure (readmission, hypoglycaemia) is what lets you show that closing the loop actually reduced harm.
